Gans. 


FOREWORD 


HE decision to raise one million, five hundred 

thousand dollars to provide Greater Montreal 

with increased facilities for the work of its 
Young Men’s Christian Association is based upon a 
survey, made in 1925, showing great unmet needs in 
the lives of men and boys as well as the family and 
community needs in certain sections of the City; a 
recognized responsibility on the part of the Young 
Men’s Christian Association to meet these needs; 
and the consciousness that Montreal is generous in 
its provision of funds for programs which further its 
civic welfare. 


Due to the rapid growth of population, large areas 
of greater Montreal are, at present, inadequately 
served by the Association. Approximately ten 
thousand boys and young men now come into contact 
with the Association each week. At least double this 
number should be provided for. 


Tuts book gives the details of the project planned to 
meet this pressing civic need—the foundation for the 
same, all the facts and figures and the reasons why 
such a project can be successfully carried out. 


Reap carefully the story given on the following 
pages. You will be impressed by the tremendous 
significance of this expansion campaign. 


zooo Men are giving their time NOW to make this 
campaign successful. Be sympathetic towards them 
and BE GENEROUS TOWARDS THE BOYS OF GREATER 
MONTREAL,

PAGE TWO 


Employment Department. One of the many “Y" services. 


Resident members at a Sunday afternoon Tea-Musicale. 


swimming pool or a night school class. While the “Y” of course is all of these, 

it uses them as a means to the end of shaping, molding, and building Christian 
character. This is its central objective, its reason for existence. No one duty or genuine 
obligation that confronts the citizens of Montreal should claim as much attention as this 
matter. Since 1851 the ““Y” in Montreal has held aloft its torch of idealism, never failing 
to show the way of truer life to the youth of our city. Such high and noble ideals must 
ever be cherished and perpetuated. 


You may have thought of the Y.M.C.A. as a gymnasium, a pleasure club, a 


Becinninc humbly from the standpoint of equipment, but with the primary purpose of 
Christian character-building, the Montreal “Y” has continually and consistently forged 
ahead. Its trained leaders help organize and furnish programs for young men and boys 
in their natural groupings throughout the community. The Montreal “Y” is now super- 
vising important community extension work in Point St. Charles, Cote St. Paul, Verdun, 
and the north-east section of the city. 


Tue Montreal Y.M.C.A. was the first organized on the North American Continent, and 
has an enviable record of seventy-seven years of service on behalf of the young men and 
boys of this community. The citizens of Montreal desire it to maintain its present 
position of influence and thus play its part as one of the major institutions of society 
in the development of Christian character and Canadian citizenship. This Expansion 
Campaign for $1,500,000.00 will assure the continuance of its influence. 1T Is NINETEEN 
YEARS SINCE THE Y.M.C.A. APPEALED FOR FUNDS FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURE.

A Bit Of “Y” History

them with the vision that makes for

St. Helen Street Baptist Church. 
It was here that the Montreal 
Y.M.C.A. was organized, in 1851. 


In 1851 The Y.M.C.A. of Montreal was organized—the first on the American 

Continent. From 1867 to 1873 it was located in the Bible House, Craig 
and St. Alexander Streets. In 1873 it entered its first building (cost $50,000) on Victoria 
Square, carrying on evangelistic meetings, educational classes, and equipped with a 
reading room and library. 


In 1891 A building was constructed on Dominion Square, on the site of the present

of the city was 
made, looking toward a fuller 
occupation of the field. Metro- 
politan Board definitely decided 
that a program of expansion 
must be entered upon.

ces a $1,500,000.00 
Expansion Campaign to 
provide a building south of the 
Lachine Canal, a building in the 
west end of the city, centering in 
Notre Dame de Grace, an Even- 
ing College and Residence build- 
ing on Stanley Street, remodel- 
ling of the Drummond Street 
building, and recreation grounds 
in the northern part of the city.

to serve the employees of the Grand Trunk Railway.

Notre Dame de Grace is the most rapidly growing English-speaking part of Mont- 
real. It now has a population of 55,000. It pays more taxes than any other re- 
sidential ward in Montreal. Yet the district has no public bath, no public skating 
rink, no public hall, no public library. In the essentials which go to make for 
healthy, happy community life it is notoriously lacking.

RESIDENCE ACCOMMODATION: 


A residence of 450 rooms is a minimum requirement. Montreal is one of the great 
gateways of Canada, not only for Europeans but for men from the United States. 
Young men are led by immigration officers and others to expect that the Y.M.C.A. 
will provide them with rooms and other accommodation. Although in 1927, 6,118 
young men resided in the Drummond Street Building, which has less than 200 
rooms, thousands of others could not be accommodated.

Young Men > 
Away 
From Home 


The Proposed Evening College and Residence Building. 


NE feature of “Y” work that is recognized each year as of increasing 
importance is the providing of residence accommodation for a pro- 
portion of those young men who must live away from home, in our 

city. To Montreal, numbers of these young men come from the farms or 
small towns in the Townships, from the Maritimes, Ontario, the other 
provinces of Canada, the United States, and many from the Old Country 
and other parts of Europe. Some go to the homes of relatives or friends, but 
the large majority have to depend on commercial boarding houses. 


Many unsophisticated boys thus come to Montreal seeking their fortunes. 
They are filled with high ideals and fired with ambition. Then, pressed by 
loneliness and impelled by the natural desire of the human being for com- 
panionship, many take the line of least resistance and the path that leads 
them into trouble. Most of them would rather live straight, but they don’t 
get a chance to make an intelligent choice. Vice 1s generally aggressive in 
its recruiting and virtue is often forced to play a passive part. 


Ir will readily be realized that the first few weeks of these newcomers in 
Montreal very largely influence what they will make out of themselves in the 
future. Can anything be more important than providing them at this crucial 
time with wholesome surroundings where they will meet worth-while young 
men associates. 


PAGE TEN 


Present Residence Conditions 


THERE are accommodations for 180 young men in the “Y” at present, 
including the rooms in North and Westmount branches. ‘The proposed 
Stanley Street Building will bring the total accommodations, in all branches, 
to 700. 


Under present conditions, young men under 30 are given the preference in 
“yn : ait 5 CONS : 

Y” residence. The average age of the men living in Central ‘““Y” now is 
24. Residence in the ““Y” is limited to three years. These regulations are 
necessary to permit using the ““Y” facilities to help those young men most 
in need of such wholesome surroundings. 


SURELY residence accommodation for 700 young men away from home is as 
small a number as Montreal should provide. 


‘‘Those of us who are working with the under-privileged class realize 
just how much we need a further great development of preventive 
work and your Association seems to be the one who can tackle this 
problem with the greatest hope of success and ultimate victory.” 


D. H. Scott, Superintendent, The Old Brewery Mission.

The Proposed Verdun Building 


(Serving Verdun, Cote St. Paul, Point St. Charles) 


Tue above building will be planned especially to meet the needs sf that great area 
south of the Lachine Canal. It will contain a swimming pool, gymnasium, community 
hall for meetings and concerts, boys’ and men’s club-rooms, recreation rooms, library, 
etc. The total cost will be $250,000.

OUT OF 35,734 WHO ATTENDED THE SCHOOLS OF THE PROTESTANT BOARD LAST YEAR, 
ONLY 45I WERE BOYS OVER I§ YEARS OF AGE. 


Do YOU Think Boys of 15 Are Ready to Face the World, 
Without Further Assistance? 


Every year the Y.M.C.A. brings thousands of boys and young men face to face with the 
problem of education. It challenges them to consider the importance of adequate train- 
ing. Numbers are assisted in the choice of suitable occupations. The “Y” helps them 
in a practical way, too, by operating a series of schools, elementary, secondary and 
commercial. 

THE ONLY EVENING HIGH SCHOOL IN MONTREAL IS AT THE “Y 


”» 


Tue “Y” has more young men and boys in its night schools than have all the ten govern- 
ment schools, operated by the Protestant Board, put together. (Ten government schools, 
844; The “Y” Schools, 945.) ‘‘“Y” School students pay 85% of the cost of their courses: 
students in the above ten government schools pay one dollar per term. 


ACCOMMODATION IS NEEDED FOR 2,000 STUDENTS: THE MINIMUM 
EQUIPMENT REQUIREMENTS ARE 30 CLASS-ROOMS, LABORATORIES, 
AND A TECHNICAL LIBRARY. 


By way of comparison: It cost over two million dollars to build the Montreal High School. 
It was paid from taxes. Last year it had 1,693 students. SURELY $150,000 IS A SMALL 
INVESTMENT TO GIVE 2,000 BOYS AND YOUNG MEN A “SECOND CHANCE” AT NIGHT.

‘Suggestions For Memorial Gifts 


ANY thoughtful persons perpetuate the memory of those dear to them, whether 
living or dead, by making gifts that will commemorate the life of the loved one 
through some worth-while project. 

Those who are contemplating such an act, and who are interested in the welfare of 
young men and boys, are invited to consider a subscription to the Building Fund of the 
Y.M.C.A. Such gifts will be used for the purpose indicated and suitable tablets provided, 
indicating the memorial thus established.
